name: Microsoft
title: Microsoft Confirms Final October 2026 Deadline For Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 ...
description:
ESU was designed as a temporary safety net Exchange Server 2016 and Exchange Server 2019 officially left support on the same date, despite being released several years apart.
Exchange Server 2019 CU14 and CU15 support an in-place upgrade to the initial Exchange Server SE release.
Exchange 2016 requires a legacy migration Exchange Server 2016 cannot be upgraded to Exchange SE by simply running the SE installer over the existing installation.
This is different from an in-place upgrade: the Exchange 2016 server itself does not become an SE server.
Organisations choosing an Exchange 2019 intermediate step must first deploy Exchange 2019 on supported hardware and Windows Server, migrate away from Exchange 2016 and then upgrade the Exchange 2019 servers to SE.
text:
Microsoft has confirmed that security updates for Exchange Server 2016 and Exchange Server 2019 will permanently end after October 2026, ruling out another extension to the temporary Extended Security Update programme protecting organisations that have not yet completed their migrations.

The decision establishes a final deadline for businesses still operating either product. Once the programme expires, Microsoft will no longer release vulnerability fixes for Exchange 2016 or 2019—even for organisations that purchased the second period of ESU coverage.

Microsoft introduced the temporary programme after both server releases reached their formal end of support on October 14, 2025. It was intended to provide a short security bridge for organisations that could not move to Exchange Server Subscription Edition or Exchange Online before the lifecycle deadline.

The company initially offered six months of additional coverage, running from October 2025 through April 2026. In April, however, it announced a separately purchased second ESU period extending protection until the end of October 2026.

That second concession prompted questions over whether Microsoft might offer another extension. The Exchange Server team has now delivered an unequivocal answer.

“There will be no further extension of Exchange 2016/2019 ESU program timeline,” Microsoft said. “Once October 2026 ends, there will be no further updates for Exchange 2016/2019, even if you currently have a Period 2 ESU.”

Microsoft’s wording means customers should treat October as a hard security boundary rather than another negotiable migration milestone. The company’s official announcement says organisations must complete their transition to Exchange Server Subscription Edition or a supported Microsoft 365 service.

ESU was designed as a temporary safety net

Exchange Server 2016 and Exchange Server 2019 officially left support on the same date, despite being released several years apart.

Exchange 2016 entered general availability in 2015. Its mainstream support period ended in October 2020, followed by extended support until October 14, 2025. Exchange 2019 was released in October 2018, reached the end of mainstream support in January 2024 and exited extended support in October 2025.

Under Microsoft’s Fixed Lifecycle Policy, the end of support normally means the termination of security updates, non-security fixes, bug fixes, time-zone updates and assisted technical support. The servers do not stop running, but their continued operation creates increasing security and compliance exposure as newly discovered vulnerabilities remain unpatched.

Microsoft’s Exchange supportability guidance consequently lists Exchange 2016 and 2019 as unsupported products, with Exchange Server Subscription Edition now the company’s supported platform for organisations retaining on-premises email infrastructure.

The ESU programme did not reverse that lifecycle status. Instead, it gave eligible customers access to selected security fixes while they completed an upgrade or cloud migration. It did not restore full product support, provide feature development or include the broader range of reliability and functionality fixes normally delivered to a supported release.

Microsoft also did not publish Exchange 2016 and 2019 ESU packages through the ordinary public distribution process. Organisations had to enrol in the programme and follow Microsoft’s procedures to obtain applicable updates.

The first period covered vulnerabilities rated Critical or Important from October 14, 2025, until April 14, 2026. Period 2, announced in April 2026, was sold separately and runs from May through October 2026. Purchasing the first period did not automatically entitle a customer to the second.

Microsoft’s Period 2 announcement made clear that the programme was aimed at organisations already making progress towards Exchange Server Subscription Edition but requiring additional time to finish.

Unsupported Exchange servers will become an expanding liability

The end of updates is particularly significant because Exchange is a high-value target for state-sponsored groups, ransomware operators and initial-access brokers.

An on-premises Exchange server is closely integrated with an organisation’s identity, messaging and directory infrastructure. Depending on its configuration, a compromised server can expose email, address-book information, authentication material and sensitive business communications. It may also give an attacker a foothold from which to move further into the Windows domain.

Exchange vulnerabilities have repeatedly been exploited in widespread attacks, sometimes before organisations could complete normal patching cycles. Internet-facing servers are especially attractive because an attacker can potentially reach them without first compromising an endpoint inside the network.

The risk will change fundamentally after October 2026. While ESU-enrolled servers can presently receive fixes for qualifying vulnerabilities, an Exchange 2016 or 2019 vulnerability discovered after the programme ends may remain permanently unpatched on those platforms.

Security controls such as web application firewalls, network segmentation, endpoint detection and response, restricted administrative access and Microsoft’s Exchange Emergency Mitigation Service may reduce particular risks, but they are not substitutes for vendor-supported security updates.

Temporary mitigations can also be incomplete or specific to one exploitation technique. They cannot guarantee protection against every future vulnerability affecting an obsolete codebase.

Running unsupported Exchange software may create additional governance difficulties. Organisations in regulated industries could have to explain why a critical messaging system no longer receives vendor security fixes. Cyber-insurance requirements, customer security questionnaires, contractual obligations and internal risk policies may also prohibit or severely restrict unsupported infrastructure.

The end of ESU therefore affects more than patch availability. It may require changes to risk registers, audit documentation, business-continuity plans and incident-response procedures.

Exchange Server Subscription Edition becomes the on-premises destination

For organisations that must retain Exchange on their own infrastructure, Microsoft’s preferred migration target is Exchange Server Subscription Edition, commonly shortened to Exchange Server SE.

Exchange SE became generally available on July 1, 2025. Rather than following the traditional model of releasing a new numbered Exchange version every several years, SE operates under Microsoft’s Modern Lifecycle Policy.

The product has no predetermined retirement date as long as customers remain licensed, run supported configurations and install required updates. Microsoft describes it as an evergreen release that will receive cumulative and security updates without another planned year-based Exchange Server successor.

According to Microsoft’s Exchange SE availability notice, the change is intended to provide continuous support for organisations with on-premises, cloud and hybrid email environments.

The licensing model is also different. Organisations must maintain qualifying subscription rights rather than treating Exchange SE as a conventional perpetual release that can remain unchanged for years.

That continuous servicing approach places greater emphasis on update discipline. Remaining supported will depend on installing cumulative updates within Microsoft’s required timeframes and maintaining compatible operating systems, .NET Framework versions, Active Directory environments and other prerequisites.

Exchange 2019 offers the simplest in-place route

The migration process depends heavily on the version and configuration currently deployed.

Exchange Server 2019 CU14 and CU15 support an in-place upgrade to the initial Exchange Server SE release. Microsoft designed this transition to resemble the installation of a cumulative update, allowing administrators to retain the existing server, configuration and databases where all prerequisites are satisfied.

Although technically less disruptive than a traditional version migration, it should not be treated as a routine patch. Administrators must confirm that each server runs a supported Exchange 2019 cumulative update, verify operating-system compatibility, review third-party integrations, back up critical data and test recovery procedures.

Microsoft recommends using the latest available cumulative and security updates before beginning. Organisations should also run the Exchange Health Checker and resolve unsupported or insecure configurations rather than carrying them into the new installation.

The in-place route does not include an in-place operating-system upgrade. Microsoft explicitly states that upgrading Windows Server between major versions while Exchange is installed is unsupported. If an organisation must move to a newer operating system or replace ageing hardware, it will generally need to deploy a new Exchange SE server and perform a traditional migration.

Microsoft provides a detailed Exchange SE upgrade guide covering both supported methods.

Exchange 2016 requires a legacy migration

Exchange Server 2016 cannot be upgraded to Exchange SE by simply running the SE installer over the existing installation.

These environments require what Microsoft calls a legacy upgrade. Administrators deploy a new server running Exchange SE—or, depending on their selected route and existing environment, introduce Exchange 2019 first—then move mailboxes, connectors, certificates, transport functions and other services before retiring the older system.

A direct legacy migration from a properly updated Exchange 2016 organisation to Exchange SE may be possible by adding new SE servers to the organisation and transferring workloads. This is different from an in-place upgrade: the Exchange 2016 server itself does not become an SE server.

Organisations choosing an Exchange 2019 intermediate step must first deploy Exchange 2019 on supported hardware and Windows Server, migrate away from Exchange 2016 and then upgrade the Exchange 2019 servers to SE.

Exchange 2013 presents an additional problem. Exchange Server SE RTM does not support coexistence with Exchange 2013, which reached the end of support in April 2023. Any remaining Exchange 2013 servers must be removed through a supported migration sequence before Exchange SE can be introduced.

The distinction is important because an incomplete or incorrectly sequenced upgrade can disrupt mail flow, client connectivity, hybrid integration and administrative functions.

Migrations involve more than moving mailboxes

An Exchange migration can appear straightforward when measured only by mailbox count, but production deployments frequently contain dependencies accumulated over many years.

Administrators must identify applications and appliances that submit mail through Exchange, including scanners, monitoring systems, business applications and multifunction printers. They must also review receive and send connectors, transport rules, accepted domains, certificates, namespaces, load balancers, antivirus integrations, journaling systems, archive platforms and backup products.

Public folders and arbitration mailboxes require particular attention. Hybrid environments must verify connectivity with Microsoft 365 and ensure that the Hybrid Configuration Wizard, OAuth configuration and mail-flow connectors remain correct after changes.

Client compatibility must also be examined. Older Outlook releases, mobile clients or line-of-business software may not behave as expected with the new environment.

Security settings should be reviewed rather than automatically duplicated. A migration provides an opportunity to remove obsolete protocols, restrict administrative interfaces, enable Extended Protection where supported and eliminate unnecessary internet exposure.

Organisations should also account for Active Directory. Exchange writes configuration data into the directory, so retiring the last legacy server without following Microsoft’s supported process can leave behind dependencies and complicate recipient management.

Exchange Online provides an alternative to maintaining servers

Microsoft is also encouraging customers to consider Exchange Online, either as a standalone service or as part of Microsoft 365.

A cloud migration transfers responsibility for maintaining the underlying Exchange server software to Microsoft. Customers continue to control identities, policies, data governance and service configuration, but they no longer patch the Exchange operating environment themselves.

Migration options include staged or cutover approaches for some smaller environments and hybrid migration for organisations requiring coexistence during a longer transition. The appropriate method depends on the existing Exchange version, directory configuration, number of mailboxes, identity model and operational requirements.

Moving to Exchange Online does not automatically mean that every Exchange-related server can be removed immediately. Organisations using Microsoft Entra Connect or retaining on-premises Active Directory may still need supported recipient-management arrangements. Administrators should follow Microsoft’s documented procedures instead of simply shutting down or deleting the final Exchange server.

A cloud move also requires assessment of data residency, compliance, retention, eDiscovery, backup, network capacity and third-party integrations. For some businesses, these considerations will justify keeping Exchange on premises. For others, eliminating responsibility for patching internet-facing email servers may significantly reduce operational risk.

Microsoft’s end-of-support roadmap directs customers towards Microsoft 365, Office 365 or Exchange Server SE and warns that unsupported installations no longer receive the ordinary protections delivered during the product lifecycle.

Organisations now have only months to complete the work

The October deadline leaves organisations with a limited migration window, especially where the project requires procurement, architectural changes or new server hardware.

A realistic migration may involve inventory and dependency discovery, licensing approval, infrastructure deployment, testing, change-control review, mailbox movement and the orderly decommissioning of legacy systems. Large or highly regulated organisations may also need disaster-recovery exercises, security assessments and formal business sign-off.

Administrators should begin by confirming every Exchange server and build present in the organisation. They should then establish whether each system is enrolled in the correct ESU period and verify that all available updates have been installed.

The next step is to select a destination architecture—Exchange SE, Exchange Online or a hybrid arrangement—and create a migration plan based on Microsoft’s supported upgrade paths.

Companies should not assume that an October migration can be postponed until the final security update arrives. Any deployment issue discovered late in the process could leave an organisation operating unsupported servers with no remaining vendor safety net.

The fact that Microsoft previously authorised a second ESU period may have encouraged some customers to expect further flexibility. Its latest announcement is intended to remove that ambiguity.

Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 will continue to function after October, but they will do so without future Microsoft security fixes. For organisations still relying on either platform, the remaining months represent the final opportunity to move before a temporary migration problem becomes a permanent security exposure.

text: Every weekday, the CNBC Investing Club with Jim Cramer releases the Homestretch — an actionable afternoon update, just in time for the last hour of trading on Wall Street. Stocks were mixed on Wednesday . The S & P 500 was basically flat in late afternoon trading, while the Nasdaq was modestly weaker. Once again, it was one of those days, with a big split within technology. While many chip stocks rallied, including Nvidia 's roughly 3% gain, software stocks lagged, and the hyperscalers that are funding the AI infrastructure buildout also moved lower. The move in software may be tied to this shocking news that OpenAI models broke out of a sandboxed testing environment, accessed the internet, and exploited a vulnerability to hack into an open source developer's network to find the information needed to pass an internal evaluation. The cybersecurity stocks, including CrowdStrike and Palo Alto Networks, got swept up in this software selling, and we think that's the wrong read . The security incident underscores the critical role these companies play in protecting enterprises as AI models become more sophisticated. CrowdStrike and Palo Alto Networks have now given back all the gains tied to IBM 's explanation last week that clients are more focused on figuring out how much they need to invest in cybersecurity (as well as paying up for tech hardware) than buying traditional mainframe servers. The OpenAI security incident could serve as a catalyst for companies to deepen their engagement with cybersecurity providers, benefiting CrowdStrike and Palo Alto Networks. Johnson & Johnson got a big regulatory win , with the FDA approving its Ottava Robotic surgical system for multiple general procedures. If you've been following along with the J & J story, you would know this approval was coming up. In May, we wrote how a clinical study evaluating the safety and performance of the system paved the way to this approval. But the reason why the stock was up 2% is that this approval came months earlier than anticipated. Cowen analysts had been expecting approval in late 2026, according to a research note. Ottava's upcoming launch positions it to compete in the robotic surgery market, long dominated by Intuitive Surgical 's da Vinci systems. MedTech was the weaker part of J & J's recent quarterly results, but management is very bullish about this new product. The company called it "one of the most significant MedTech innovations we will bring to market this decade." title: J&J's Ottava milestone shows how 'innovation is not a straight line' - MassDevice
description:
Nearly six years after first unveiling its Ottava soft-tissue robotics platform, Johnson & Johnson (NYSE:JNJ) has finally cleared a major regulatory hurdle.
J&J said at the time that the delays reflected technical development challenges and COVID-19-related disruptions, including supply chain constraints experienced broadly across all industries.
Its unified architecture allows for an invisible design, J&J says.
Johnson & Johnson wants to build beyond traditional surgical robotics with these digital capabilities, enabling automation and more.
Johnson & Johnson also currently has a U.S. clinical trial underway for Ottava in inguinal hernia procedures.
text:
Nearly six years after first unveiling its Ottava soft-tissue robotics platform, Johnson & Johnson (NYSE:JNJ) has finally cleared a major regulatory hurdle.

The medtech giant announced FDA de novo authorization for Ottava on Wednesday, marking the first regulatory nod for the robot, which makes it the first table-integrated soft-tissue robotics system given the FDA’s green light.

Ottava is the latest of a few long-awaited entries to the surgical robotic market, including Medtronic’s Hugo, which earned its first FDA nod for urologic procedures in December 2025.

J&J initially unveiled Ottava in 2020 as a potential minimally invasive surgical robotic option to rival longtime soft-tissue robotics leader Intuitive Surgical. After some development timeline delays raised questions about the platform, the approval finally allows the company to bring Ottava to the U.S. market, initially for a range of general surgery procedures.

“This is an incredible moment for our organization, not only for the Ottava team, many of our team members have been on this journey for a while, but most importantly for the whole Johnson and Johnson organization,” Rocco De Bernardis, global president, Ottava, told MassDevice in an interview. We’ve been leading surgery for 140 years. We were born in surgery. For us, Ottava is an opportunity to restate our leadership in surgery and bring it into the future.”

The journey to this point

After the initial unveiling, the company remained quiet about Ottava before it pushed back the platform’s development timeline by about two years due to multiple factors in late 2021.

J&J said at the time that the delays reflected technical development challenges and COVID-19-related disruptions, including supply chain constraints experienced broadly across all industries.

Once on track, though, the company announced that it submitted Ottava for FDA investigational device exemption (IDE) in October 2024. Less than a month later, the FDA approved that IDE, allowing the company to kick off a bariatric surgery study.

J&J submitted the robot to the FDA for de novo approval in January. In May, the company said Ottava met its endpoints in a pivotal study. Finally, on July 22, the long-awaited authorization arrived.

“When you are trying to do something so disruptive and so innovative, innovation is not a straight line,” De Bernardis said. “We had to navigate that.”

De Bernardis said J&J wanted to address the key challenges of surgical robotics by driving better visibility, communication, workflows and efficiency.

Doing all of this in a smaller surgical robot that integrates its arms into the surgical table was the biggest hurdle to clear.

“This is a complex engineering problem that we had to solve for,” he explained. “Our intent was to take on a complex engineering problem to bring simplicity back to surgeon and surgical teams. … That was not an easy problem to solve and I couldn’t be prouder of our R&D teams and our innovators that were able to develop on such a challenge.”

Where Ottava fits in within the surgical robotics space

Ottava’s de novo authorization highlights that there is no predicate on the market. While the first table-integrated soft-tissue robot will compete against the other platforms, like da Vinci and Hugo, it brings a different option to surgeons.

“We couldn’t be more excited about what we’re bringing to market today,” De Bernardis said. “It’s indisputably something that is very differentiated versus what it exists today, and we can be more confident that that’s going to help us establish leadership in this space.”

Ottava incorporates four robotic arms into a standard-size surgical table. Its unified architecture allows for an invisible design, J&J says. The robotic arms are available when needed and stowed beneath the surgical table when not. It occupies 30–50% less space than traditional boom- and cart-mounted systems, the company says.

“That means that the robot is a table and the table is a robot,” De Bernardis said. “There are no booms, no carts, which is basically where soft-tissue robotics has been stuck to a certain extent from a design standpoint.”

The technology also connects with the Polyphonic digital ecosystem to support teams throughout the Ottava experience. Polyphonic brings learning, media and data-driven insights together to support continuous improvement across the surgical journey.

Johnson & Johnson wants to build beyond traditional surgical robotics with these digital capabilities, enabling automation and more.

“Automation, from day one, is going to be a main component of how we’re planning to innovate in this space and really remove again some of the manual steps and friction that exist in the operating room,” De Bernardis said.

What’s next for Johnson & Johnson and Ottava

The FDA nod for Ottava covers general procedures such as Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, gastrectomy, cholecystectomy, splenectomy, gastric sleeve, small bowel resection, appendectomy, lysis of adhesions, fundoplication, and hiatal hernia repair.

Johnson & Johnson also currently has a U.S. clinical trial underway for Ottava in inguinal hernia procedures.

“We have, in every indication we’re delivering to the market, areas of innovation and differentiation that surgeons are telling us about,” De Bernardis said. “At the same time, we also understand that it’s important for Ottava to be a multi-specialty robotic system. Ultimately, hospitals are making an investment in our technologies, and they want to make sure that we can drive utilization for them. Being a multi-specialty robotic system is definitely a key part of that.”

J&J plans to commercially launch Ottava with select customers in the U.S. It said it intends to focus on early customer success while working to advance into additional indications and regulatory jurisdictions over time.

“We understand that one of the key things for us to begin with is working with leading, highly reputable institutions in the U.S.,” De Bernardis said. “[We want to] partner with them and make sure that we drive customer success for them, and make them very happy with our technology. They can help us and continue to challenge us on the innovation pipeline that we have designed for the next 3-5 years.”

De Bernardis concluded by calling the milestone a “very special moment” for everyone at J&J and within the Ottava team.

“[Ottava] is something that is definitely going to make an impact in the marketplace, and we cannot wait to work with leading institutions and surgeons that have been working with us for many years to really make an impact and a difference for patients through surgical treatments,” he said.

title: J&J's OTTAVA Robot Gets FDA Nod, Challenges Intuitive

text:
After nearly a decade of build up, Johnson & Johnson has announced FDA De Novo authorization for the OTTAVA Robotic Surgical System, the world’s first table-integrated soft tissue robotic system.

FDA has granted the device marketing authorization for multiple procedures in general surgery, including Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, gastrectomy, cholecystectomy, splenectomy, gastric sleeve, small bowel resection, appendectomy, lysis of adhesions, fundoplication, and hiatal hernia repair.

Johnson & Johnson plans to roll out the OTTAVA system through a controlled commercial launch with select U.S. customers, prioritizing early adoption success while simultaneously pursuing expanded indications and international regulatory approvals.

The company is also conducting a U.S. clinical trial evaluating OTTAVA for inguinal hernia procedures.

“"This is an incredible moment for not only the OTTAVA team, but the whole Johnson & Johnson organization," Rocco De Bernardis, Global President of OTTAVA, told MD+DI.

"It's very differentiated versus anything else that is available on the market today. It is the world's first table-integrated soft tissue robotic system. It's the way we're signaling to the market that we're planning to extend our 140 years of leadership in surgery and really co-create with leading surgeons around the world what's next in surgery and start to get a new era for surgery."

OTTAVA system designed for current and future surgical needs

OTTAVA is designed to address both current surgical needs and future innovations. The system's distinctive architecture, automation capabilities, advanced robotic instruments, and integration with an open digital ecosystem allow it to fit into today's operating rooms while supporting the evolution toward more digitally connected, data-driven surgical care.

As hospitals work to advance surgical care while managing constraints around infrastructure, OR efficiency, data access, and rising demand for robotic-assisted procedures, OTTAVA aims to address these challenges with features designed to expand OR capacity, streamline workflows, improve data visibility, and broaden access to robotic surgery.

Key features of J&J's robotic surgical platform

Key features of the first-generation system include a compact footprint: OTTAVA integrates robotic arms directly into the OR table, occupying 30–50% less space than traditional boom- and cart-mounted systems.

Automation capabilities: Sophisticated software coordinates the four table-integrated arms, enabling automated, pre-defined procedural positions to simplify setup and breakdown.

Advanced instrumentation: Drawing on decades of experience in open and laparoscopic surgery, J&J has redesigned commonly used surgical tools for robotic applications. Notable innovations include a two-in-one needle driver engineered to reduce unintended suture cutting and monopolar curved scissors designed for consistent, complete cuts.

Digital integration: OTTAVA connects to J&J's Polyphonic digital ecosystem, a secure platform that consolidates learning resources, media, and data-driven insights to support continuous improvement throughout the surgical process.

Comprehensive training: Leveraging J&J's educational expertise, the OTTAVA training program was developed with clinicians, educational specialists, and surgical societies. The curriculum supports both new and experienced robotic surgeons through virtual, hands-on, and immersive training designed to ensure safe adoption and consistent performance.

Johnson & Johnson first announced Ottava in late 2020; a moment that many investors and industry professionals had been waiting for.

Johnson & Johnson is making a calculated entry into the surgical robotics market at a time when Intuitive Surgical has maintained dominant control for more than two decades, holding approximately 80% market share with its da Vinci system.

While several competitors—including Medtronic with Hugo, CMR Surgical with Versius, and others—have attempted to challenge Intuitive's position with varying degrees of success, J&J is leveraging its century-long legacy in surgical innovation, global scale, and deep relationships with hospitals and surgeons to differentiate its approach.

As a result of the announcement, shares for both Intuitive Surgical and Medtronic have declined.

The company is positioning OTTAVA not as a direct da Vinci competitor, but as a "new category" in soft tissue robotics, emphasizing its space-saving table-integrated design, automation features, and connection to an open digital ecosystem as key differentiators.

"We're not sharing specific details on the commercial plans, but what I can tell you is that we might not be the first, we're not definitely the first in this space, but we're coming to market to lead in this space," De Bernardis said. "And we have very bold plans for OTTAVA and beyond to extend our leadership in surgery into robotics."

Surgical robotics market presents high barriers to entry

This strategic framing, combined with J&J's controlled commercial launch focused on early customer success, suggests the company is taking a measured, long-term approach to capturing market share in one of medtech's most lucrative but challenging segments, particularly as the cautionary tale of Vicarious Surgical's recent dissolution underscores the significant barriers to entry in surgical robotics.

"Having the backing of J&J in such a venture is definitely an advantage," De Bernardis noted when asked about Vicarious Surgical's dissolution.

"And, to be able to succeed in this market, it requires commitment, resilience, and commitment also from an investment standpoint. It takes time to innovate, especially in our case where we decided to go a very different route from an architecture and innovation standpoint."

In May, Intuitive Surgical rolled out over 100 updates to its da Vinci 5 robotic surgery platform — including enhanced telepresence, extended-use instruments, and improved cybersecurity — as the company began facing faster-growing competition from Medtronic and J&J.

In addition, Metronic recently filed submission to FDA for Hugo RAS for the general surgery and gynecologic indications.

Table-integrated design creates new category in robotic surgery

When asked what makes OTTAVA a category creator rather than just another competitor, De Bernardis explained: "If you look at the current configuration architectures that are available today, they are either boom-based or cart-based, and they all require a lot of manual intervention by the surgical team. They occupy a lot of space. They hinder visibility and communication. They're complex to manage and adopting robotic systems is not an easy task for surgical teams around the world."

"OTTAVA not only brings a minimal footprint into the operating room, 30% to 50% smaller than any robotic leading robotic system out there, it also brings automation from day one," he continued.

"And automation is going to be a key component of our future innovation. OTTAVA is a platform that is meant to evolve over time, to grow its capabilities, and automation is definitely one of the key components of that. And the way we're thinking about it is how we simplify the utilization, set up, turn down, turnover of a robotic OR, and how we make every OR a robotic OR through our capabilities."

Robotic arms integrate into OR table to reduce surgical friction

The table-integrated design that J&J has championed represents a fundamental departure from traditional robotic surgery architecture.

By integrating the robotic arms directly into the operating table rather than using separate booms or carts, OTTAVA aims to reduce what Hani Abouhalka, group chairman of surgery and robotics at J&J MedTech, describes as "the tension and friction between the surgical team and the robot."

This approach allows the arms to retract invisibly when not needed, enabling the same OR to serve open, laparoscopic, and robotic procedures without requiring dedicated robotic suites.

"Right now, if you go to a hospital, robotic ORs have to be dedicated to robotics. We believe that ORs should be ORs to serve all surgery, whether it's open, laparoscopic, and robotics," De Bernardis said.

"Our solution, OTTAVA, the arms are integrated on the table. When you don't need them, they're stored invisibly, you don't see them. When you need them, you can deploy one or multiple arms based on the need of the surgery."

De Bernardis emphasized the importance of bringing J&J's instrumentation legacy to robotics: "The third element that is important, that's going to be really differentiating ourselves is our ability to bring a wealth of clinical expertise and innovation from Ethicon on to OTTAVA. This is what surgeons have been demanding for many, many years. And we're excited about the fact that we've integrated innovation pipelines in our team to drive innovation across open lab and robotics consistently so that surgeons using our technologies know what to expect. They know and trust that we're going to deliver to them our best technologies."

With 25% of surgeries still resulting in post-operative complications, J&J believes that bringing trusted instrumentation and consistent performance across open, laparoscopic, and robotic approaches will differentiate OTTAVA both clinically and economically. This strategy reflects the company's confidence that it can "disrupt and change surgery" as it has for the past 140 years.

Digital ecosystem integration sets OTTAVA apart

Beyond hardware, J&J is betting on digital integration as a key differentiator. "Last but not least, we have integrated OTTAVA with our polyphonic ecosystem, our open and secure digital ecosystem around OTTAVA," De Bernardis explained.

"This is the application that surgeons are going to use who are now interacting with OTTAVA. This is how they prepare for a procedure. This is how they're going to be learning and be better in what they do in their practice. This is how we're going to be collecting data from very different data sources, from J&J devices, non-J&J devices in the operating room, and turning those data points that today are completely unutilized into meaningful insights for them."

"We're also open to innovation. We're open to third parties, to surgical innovators who want to use the data that we're going to be providing to them to drive automation, AI, new algorithms, and new solutions for surgery. So it becomes really a platform for innovation as well," he added.

Clinical trial results support FDA authorization

FDA authorization follows promising results from OTTAVA's first clinical study, a prospective, multicenter trial evaluating the system's safety and performance in Roux-en-Y gastric bypass procedures.

Presented at the 2026 American Society for Metabolic and Bariatric Surgery annual meeting in May, the 30-patient study met its primary safety and performance endpoints through 30 days post-procedure, with all procedures completed robotically without conversion to a non-robotic approach.

In five of the six sites, procedures were performed in ORs that had never been used for robotic surgery, including rooms previously considered too space-constrained for robotic systems.

"These results further illustrate how novel architecture supports a differentiated approach where it matters most: in real operating rooms, with real patients," said Peter Schulam, MD, PhD, chief scientific officer in J&J's MedTech division. "At each step—from bench to preclinical and now human trial—we have observed that this system can allow more hospital ORs to accommodate robotics."

Controlled U.S. launch strategy prioritizes customer success

J&J's approach to commercialization reflects lessons learned from watching competitors enter the market. "We understand that this is a very different technology, and we want to make sure that, first of all, we partner with leading institutions in the U.S. who are experts in robotic surgery. That's really the key important step," De Bernardis said. "We want to drive success for them, making sure that we work with them on providing additional evidence around our value proposition and differentiation, whether it's economic or clinical."

"We want to upgrade the system that is going to be in the field for them with new capabilities. OTTAVA, as I mentioned before, is a platform that is going to grow tremendously at a steady pace with new features, software capabilities, and new instrumentation," he continued. "And last but not least, we understand that OTTAVA has to be a multi-specialty robotic system. And so we're planning to expand very quickly with approved indications through additional clinical trials."

When asked about lessons learned from competitors, De Bernardis noted: "One of the things that we're definitely doing differently versus other companies is, one, we're starting in the U.S. This is the biggest, most consolidated market with the biggest experts in robotic surgery in the world. We're starting here because the opportunity is bigger, but also because we feel confident that we can go ahead and compete from day one. The second element is that we have chosen to go into general surgery, which is a less penetrated segment of the market. And quite frankly, a segment where we have a very strong legacy and equity with our customers who have been on a journey with us for so many years."

Automation features simplify OR setup and workflow

One of OTTAVA's most distinctive features is its automation capabilities, whichDe Bernardis described in detail: "With boom-based systems or cart-based systems, there is a lot of manual interaction with the system. The surgical team has to do a lot to set up the system properly at the beginning of the procedure and tear it down at the end of the procedure. With OTTAVA, we're able to set up the system through automated procedure poses based upon the specific procedure in the patient that the surgeon is treating that day. So there is no calibration, registration, there is no movement of components around the surgical table."

"By pressing a button, the position, the arms, our intelligent surgical arms go into a docking position, which is 90% the way that, you know, the ultimate position of those intelligent surgical arms. This removes a lot of variability in the surgical theater, allowing even less expert surgical team members to set it up. You don't have to have your A-team all the time in the surgical OR with you. It's so simple that pretty much anyone could be maneuvering it with sufficient training," he explained.

The system's Twin Motion feature further enhances workflow efficiency. "In the case of Twin Motion, the synchronized table motion, we're restoring the natural movement of general surgeons using our surgical system. With OTTAVA, synchronized table motion comes for every single patient with no interruption, no additional steps in the procedure. Again, it's all about ensuring uninterrupted flow in the procedure. Once you set it up, you go, you don't have to stop the procedure, adjust the system, and restart the procedure. So again, it contributes not only to the clinical benefits for the patient with easier exposure of critical structure and organs that the surgeon needs to operate, but also efficiency in the operating room at the speed at which a procedure can be performed."

J&J confident in comprehensive competitive advantage

When asked about J&J's competitive advantage beyond hardware, De Bernardis expressed confidence in the company's comprehensive approach: "What my confidence is related to, first of all, the unique architecture, the integrated architecture, and some of the elements that I mentioned before. The talent that we have assembled around the technology, the investment and commitment from a J&J standpoint. And last but not least, what's resonating a lot with hospital systems and surgeons who have been with us on the journey is that yes, we're going to be bringing a very differentiated technology, disruptive, one-of-a-kind technology to the market, but we're also thinking more broadly about surgery with open lab robotic procedures at the center, and we'll continue innovating across all of those modalities. So all of that, plus our expertise in commercial, regulatory affairs, service, training, which is still an unmet need, makes me very confident that we're going to be leaders in this space."

OTTAVA positioned as evolving platform for surgical innovation

With FDA authorization secured and initial clinical data demonstrating both safety and practical feasibility in space-constrained operating rooms, Johnson & Johnson is positioning OTTAVA as more than just another robotic surgical system—it's a platform designed to evolve.

The company's emphasis on automation, digital integration, and bringing its legacy Ethicon instrumentation to robotics signals a long-term vision that extends beyond hardware innovation to encompass the entire surgical ecosystem.

As J&J begins its controlled U.S. launch with select customers and continues clinical trials for additional indications, the surgical robotics market, long dominated by a single player, is entering a new era of competition.

Whether OTTAVA can deliver on its promise to make every OR a robotic OR and capture meaningful market share will depend not only on the technology itself, but on J&J's ability to execute on training, service, and the continuous innovation it has pledged.

For hospitals struggling with space constraints, efficiency demands, and the growing expectation for robotic-assisted surgery, OTTAVA represents a fundamentally different approach—one that could reshape how surgical teams think about integrating robotics into their daily practice.

text:
The news: Nationwide gained 65,000 current account customers in Q1 2026—more than three times as many as Barclays and over five times Lloyds, per MoneyWeek. This follows the building society’s November 2025 "Branch Promise" not to close any of its nearly 700 branches until 2030 at the earliest. CEO Debbie Crosbie said Nationwide is also considering opening new branches in select locations.

Zooming out: Nationwide is finding success with its branch network strategy. In May, it reported a 20% jump in account openings tied to in-branch visits in the trailing year.

This comes even as UK in-branch banking users industrywide are set to fall nearly 20% between 2025 and 2029, per our forecast. Nationwide's shareholder-owned rivals keep shrinking their branch networks accordingly:

Barclays plans to close 166 branches in 2026 and 2027, per Moneyweek.

Lloyds has closed 397 branches since March 2022, per Moneyweek.

Nationwide's current account growth may also stem from its mutual structure—comparable to a US credit union—which allows it to return profits directly to members rather than shareholders, allowing it to fund loyalty payments like its £100 ($134) "Fairer Share" bonus. It most recently paid the bonus to more than 4 million customers in June, the fourth consecutive year it has done so. Those payments reinforce Nationwide's value proposition and give consumers another tangible reason to switch or stay beyond rates and products.

Why it matters: UK financial institutions are reevaluating branches’ role in acquisition and retention, even despite declining visits. Other building societies are following Nationwide’s lead: Cumberland Building Society pledged in July to keep all 31 of its branches open, and Newcastle Building Society has invested more than £12 million ($16.05 million) in its branch network since 2015. Among shareholder-owned banks, Santander pledged not to close any of its 480 branches before 2028, and HSBC promised the same through at least 2027.

Implications for banks: Nationwide's current account gains suggest that both branch access and tangible financial rewards are significant competitive differentiators. The latter gives building societies with mutual structures an inherent edge that digital and shareholder-owned competitors cannot easily replicate.

On the branch front, banks that have leaned hardest into closures may need to compete more aggressively on pricing, service, or digital features to offset the loss of physical access.

Revenue above EUR 41 billion

According to the companys published annual figures for fiscal 2023, L'Oréal reported group sales in excess of EUR 41 billion, marking a clear increase compared with the prior-year period when revenue had been several billion euros lower. This expansion reflects not only price and mix effects but also higher volumes in strategic segments, including luxury fragrances, professional haircare, and mass-market skincare sold through retail and e-commerce channels worldwide.

Within that topline, management has highlighted particularly strong momentum in dermatological beauty, a category that includes specialist skincare brands distributed via pharmacies, dermatologists, and medical channels. In the most recent full-year reporting cycle, dermatological beauty sales grew by more than 20 percent year on year, outpacing the companys overall growth rate and underlining how targeted medical skincare has become a key driver of L'Oréal's structural expansion in the global beauty market.

Dermatological beauty grows more than 20 percent

The more than 20 percent year-on-year rise in dermatological beauty revenue in 2023 compares with a lower double-digit percentage increase in consolidated group sales over the same period, illustrating how this segment is gaining share inside L'Oréal's portfolio. The company has attributed this performance to product innovation in areas such as sun protection, sensitive-skin formulations, and acne treatment, as well as continued geographic expansion in markets where dermatologist-recommended skincare is still underpenetrated.

On a regional basis, L'Oréal's 2023 figures show that revenues in Asia and North America grew faster than in Western Europe, offering diversification benefits for the group. The company has reported mid- to high-single-digit sales growth in its home European markets, whereas several Asian markets, including China, delivered growth rates in the low- to mid-teens in percentage terms year on year. This regional mix supports the overall growth profile and has helped offset slower dynamics in certain mature markets where consumers face higher living costs and more cautious discretionary spending.

Profitability has remained robust alongside the topline expansion. In fiscal 2023, L'Oréal generated operating profit in the mid-single-digit billions of euros, with an operating margin above 20 percent, broadly in line with or slightly higher than the level achieved in the previous year. The company has managed to absorb higher input costs and increased marketing investments while maintaining a margin profile that compares favorably with many consumer-goods peers, reflecting both brand pricing power and disciplined cost management.

Operating margin above 20 percent

The operating margin above 20 percent in 2023 represents a modest improvement versus the prior year, when L'Oréal's margin had been just under this threshold. The increase illustrates how the company has leveraged scale and premiumization to offset cost inflation in areas such as packaging, raw materials, and logistics. As a result, the incremental profit contribution from each additional euro of sales has remained attractive, supporting cash generation and the capacity to invest in research, digital channels, and selective acquisitions.

L'Oréal's financial structure remains conservative. At the end of fiscal 2023, the company reported a net cash or low net-debt position measured in the low-single-digit billions of euros, after accounting for cash and equivalents on the balance sheet. This balance-sheet strength enables ongoing shareholder returns, including dividends and share buybacks, while preserving flexibility to fund future strategic initiatives. The group has historically distributed a significant portion of its earnings via dividends, with the most recent full-year dividend representing a cash outlay of more than EUR 3 billion to shareholders.

From a market perspective, the share price performance over the past year has reflected the combination of steady earnings growth and a premium valuation multiple typical of quality consumer-brand companies. As of a recent trading day in mid-2026, L'Oréal's equity value implied a market capitalization in the range of EUR 200 billion to EUR 250 billion, positioning the company among the largest constituents of major European indices and underscoring its role as a core holding in many global consumer and equity-income portfolios.

Flagship brands support premium pricing

A key driver behind L'Oréal's ability to grow sales and margins simultaneously is its diversified brand portfolio spanning mass-market and luxury segments. The group owns internationally recognized labels in makeup, skincare, haircare, and fragrance, ranging from accessible brands sold through supermarkets and drugstores to high-end lines available in department stores and dedicated boutiques. This breadth allows the company to address different price points and demographics while leveraging cross-category marketing campaigns and global distribution partnerships.

Innovation and marketing remain central to the growth strategy. L'Oréal invests a significant proportion of its annual revenue in research and development, amounting to over EUR 1 billion in 2023, to develop new formulations, packaging, and technology-driven beauty solutions. At the same time, the group has steadily increased its allocation to digital advertising and social-media campaigns, reflecting the shift in consumer discovery and purchase behavior toward online platforms and influencers. The combination of proprietary science and strong brand storytelling helps sustain premium pricing and customer loyalty.

In e-commerce, the company has reported double-digit sales growth year on year, with online channels now representing a meaningful share of total revenue. The growth has been fueled by direct-to-consumer websites, partnerships with major online retailers, and targeted campaigns on social platforms. As a result, L'Oréal has become less dependent on traditional brick-and-mortar retail, giving it more resilience against changes in footfall patterns and allowing for richer first-party data collection, which can be used to optimize product launches and marketing messages.

Beauty Tech and omnichannel strategy

Beyond traditional product development, L'Oréal has positioned itself as a Beauty Tech player, integrating digital tools into its offering and operations. The company has rolled out virtual try-on technology for makeup and hair color, enabling consumers to see how products might look using augmented reality on smartphones or in-store devices. It also deploys artificial intelligence and data analytics to refine shade ranges, customize skincare recommendations, and optimize assortments by region and retailer. These investments support higher conversion rates online and in stores, further reinforcing revenue growth.

The omnichannel strategy extends to logistics and supply chain. L'Oréal has invested in automated distribution centers and demand-forecasting systems to ensure product availability across regions while managing inventory efficiently. By aligning production and inventory with real-time demand signals from physical and digital channels, the company aims to reduce stockouts and markdowns, which can otherwise pressure margins. The result is a more agile organization capable of responding quickly to trends, such as surging demand for specific skincare ingredients or seasonal makeup collections.

Environmental and social initiatives form another pillar of L'Oréal's long-term strategy. The company has set targets to reduce greenhouse-gas emissions, water consumption, and waste in its operations, alongside commitments to sustainable sourcing of key ingredients such as palm oil derivatives and certain botanical extracts. It has also introduced refillable packaging concepts in selected product lines and expanded recycling partnerships to lower the environmental footprint of its products. These steps are not only cost and risk management measures but also respond to growing consumer expectations for responsible corporate behavior.

Skincare line anchors growth

Within L'Oréal's broad portfolio, its skincare line has been a standout contributor to growth, both in mass-market and premium segments. The company continues to launch new serums, moisturizers, and targeted treatments addressing concerns such as aging, hyperpigmentation, and sensitivity, often backed by clinical studies and dermatologist endorsements. Over the past several years, skincare has increased its share of total group revenue, reflecting both higher average selling prices and rising consumer interest in multi-step routines and preventative care.

L'Oréal's skincare products are distributed through multiple channels, including pharmacies, specialty retailers, department stores, and online platforms. This channel mix allows the company to reach consumers seeking efficacy-led, scientifically backed formulations as well as those drawn to luxury brand experiences and packaging. In emerging markets, the expansion of pharmacy networks and rising middle-class incomes offer additional runway for growth, particularly in sun-care and dermocosmetic ranges tailored to local skin types and climate conditions.

L'Oréal stock and market positioning

L'Oréal stock trades on Euronext Paris and is included in major indices such as the CAC 40, reflecting its status as a large-cap European consumer company with a global footprint. As of a recent trading session in 2026, the share price on Euronext Paris assigned the company a market capitalization comfortably above EUR 200 billion, underlining its role as one of the most valuable beauty and personal-care companies worldwide. The stock's valuation typically embeds expectations of continued mid- to high-single-digit annual sales growth and stable to slightly expanding margins over the medium term.

For investors, the combination of consistent earnings growth, strong cash generation, and a disciplined capital-allocation policy is central to the investment case around L'Oréal stock. The companys track record of investing through cycles in brands, innovation, and technology, while maintaining a solid balance sheet and regular shareholder distributions, positions it as a defensive yet growth-oriented name within the global consumer sector.

text:
By Elias Schisgall

A federal judge blocked New York City from enforcing a law requiring ride-share companies to demonstrate "just cause" to deactivate driver accounts in a victory for Uber and Lyft.

In lawsuits last month, the companies claimed that New York's Local Law 52 violated the terms of their contracts with drivers by setting a series of conditions on when accounts can be deactivated. They asked a court to grant a preliminary injunction blocking the law before it took effect on July 28.

Judge Gregory Woods granted that request in a Tuesday ruling, writing that Uber's and Lyft's arguments were likely to prevail in court and barring the city from enforcing the law until a further court order.

"Uber and Lyft are likely to succeed in showing that the law protects a narrow class of drivers and does not advance the broader social or economic interest which the Constitution requires to permit the severe impairment of their contracts," Woods wrote.

Representatives for the New York City Law Department didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

Local Law 52 would have required Uber, Lyft, and other ride-share companies to show that a driver whose account was deactivated had engaged in "egregious misconduct" or been recently disciplined. It also required a 14-day notice before any deactivation and allowed drivers to petition for reinstatement.

The law was passed in January over the veto of former Mayor Eric Adams.

text:
Johnson & Johnson has officially entered the US soft-tissue robotic surgery market after receiving marketing authorisation from the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for its Ottava robotic surgical system. It is a major milestone in the healthcare giant's effort to challenge established players in robotic-assisted surgery.

The authorisation allows J&J to begin a phased commercial rollout of the Ottava system in the United States, initially targeting select healthcare providers.

Reuters reported that the approval positions the company to compete more directly with market leader Intuitive Surgical and Medtronic in the rapidly expanding surgical robotics segment.

FDA Clears Ottava For Multiple Surgical Procedures

The FDA has authorised the Ottava robotic surgical system for use in several upper abdominal general surgery procedures, including:

Gastric bypass surgery

Gastrectomy

Gallbladder removal

Gastric sleeve surgery

Appendectomy

Hiatal hernia repair

Johnson & Johnson have plans to gradually expand the system's approved uses while pursuing regulatory approvals in additional international markets.

J&J Eyes Global Expansion

The company said its long-term strategy extends beyond the US market.

Hani Abouhalka, Chairman of Surgery at J&J MedTech, said the company intends to become a leader in surgical robotics while accelerating launches in major international markets, including Japan and Western Europe.

He added that robotic-assisted procedures currently account for only about 8% of surgeries worldwide, leaving significant room for future growth as hospitals increasingly adopt robotic technology.

ALSO READ: US Stock Market Today: Nasdaq Jumps 1% On Chip Rally

What Makes Ottava Different?

Unlike conventional robotic surgery platforms, Ottava integrates its robotic arms directly into the operating table rather than using separate boom-and-cart-mounted systems.

According to Johnson & Johnson, this design reduces the system's operating room footprint by around 30% to 50%, potentially allowing hospitals with limited space to introduce robotic-assisted surgery where it was previously impractical.

The company believes the compact design could improve workflow efficiency and expand access to robotic procedures.

Tough Competition Awaits

Despite the regulatory milestone, analysts believe Johnson & Johnson faces an uphill battle in winning market share.

The robotic surgery market is currently dominated by Intuitive Surgical's da Vinci system, which has built a strong presence in hospitals over the past two decades through an extensive installed base, physician training programmes and established clinical workflows.

Medtronic also entered the market after receiving US approval for its Hugo robotic-assisted surgery system last year.

J.P. Morgan analyst Robbie Marcus noted that while Ottava offers advantages such as a smaller footprint, many surgeons continue to favour Intuitive Surgical because of its deep relationships with physicians and widespread integration into hospital systems and academic medical centres.

He also suggested that Johnson & Johnson, like Medtronic, may wait until it secures approval for urology procedures before pursuing a broader commercial rollout.

Growth Opportunity In Surgical Robotics

Industry analysts expect robotic-assisted surgery to remain one of the fastest-growing areas within medical technology as hospitals increasingly invest in minimally invasive procedures that can improve surgical precision, shorten recovery times and enhance patient outcomes.

TD Cowen analyst Michael Nedelcovych said Johnson & Johnson could file another US regulatory submission as early as next year after completing clinical studies for inguinal hernia repair, one of the most commonly performed surgeries in the country.

With the FDA authorisation now secured, Johnson & Johnson has taken its first major step into a market that is expected to see continued innovation and growing competition over the coming years.

text:
TORONTO, ON and REDMOND, Wash. — Manulife and Microsoft today announced the renewal and expansion of their longstanding relationship, supporting Manulife’s strategic priority to become an AI-powered organization. As part of this partnership, Manulife has adopted Microsoft 365 E7 Frontier Suite capabilities to enable innovation at scale with secure cloud and AI solutions. This includes expanding adoption of Microsoft 365 Copilot to over 30,000 employees and deploying Microsoft Agent 365 – a next-generation suite that provides a control plane for governing, monitoring, and securing AI agents at enterprise scale. The five-year agreement supports Manulife’s continued transformation and responsible scaling of AI-enabled capabilities across its global operations.

“Our partnership with Microsoft is a critical enabler of Manulife’s continued evolution into a truly AI-powered organization,” said Shamus Weiland, Chief Technology & Operations Officer, Manulife. “Adopting the Microsoft Frontier Suite represents the next phase of that transformation, giving us the trusted foundation to advance AI across our global operations with confidence. It also provides the scale, security, stability and intelligence we need to accelerate innovation and embed AI responsibly across the franchise.”

A secure, governed foundation for enterprise AI

Microsoft is a foundational partner in Manulife’s global enterprise AI platform, currently in pilot, which will help to enable Manulife’s data scientists and developers to build, deploy and manage advanced AI and agentic solutions at scale, while adhering to shared standards for quality, security and cost efficiency. Microsoft Azure and Microsoft Foundry provide critical components and capabilities ranging from citizen development tools to advanced model fine-tuning and monitoring, enabling teams to innovate autonomously within a strong governance framework.

Manulife will also deploy Microsoft Agent 365, to serve as a registry for AI agents across the enterprise, providing a single interface to observe, govern, and manage how AI agents operate. This capability will help Manulife’s enterprise-wide approach to AI governance, observability, and risk management.

“As AI becomes more deeply embedded across our business, responsible innovation has to be built into how we operate — not treated as a separate layer of oversight,” said Jodie Wallis, Global Chief AI Officer, Manulife. “For Manulife, that means giving our teams the clarity, controls and confidence to use AI in ways that are secure, transparent and aligned to our Responsible AI Principles. By strengthening how we govern and monitor AI across the enterprise, we can move with greater speed and discipline while continuing to earn the trust of our customers, colleagues and communities.”

Examples of AI solutions already enabled by Microsoft technology across the business include:

Revenue growth: The Sales Enablement tool, launched in Singapore and now scaled across multiple markets, delivers personalized advisor insights using Foundry models, driving more targeted engagement and improved sales outcomes.

Underwriting support: Quick Quote, a GenAI based underwriting support tool launched by John Hancock in the U.S., which helps streamline the preliminary assessment process for purchasing life insurance.

Customer experience: Generative AI solutions support over 110 million calls annually across North America and are expanding into Asia, enhancing speed, accuracy, and service quality through Azure-based knowledge tools that provide instant, source-backed answers with confidence scores.

Additionally, Manulife has agentic solutions and AI-powered workflows live in production across the organization, with more in the pipeline. Agents can help employees quickly access information, support software development and technology design, and enhance IT operations by streamlining workflows, identifying risks, and improving productivity across the organization.

Accelerating innovation across the enterprise

Manulife developers across the organization continue to adopt assisted and autonomous AI capabilities and have increased their productivity by 30 per cent while enabling reinvestment to support business growth and develop new capabilities to serve our customers. GitHub Copilot has helped lay a strong foundation for the next phase of Manulife’s AI strategy, by advancing Manulife’s autonomous development capabilities, supporting faster design, build and release processes. This includes business-facing solutions such as Manulife’s mortgage renewal application, which was successfully rebuilt in a matter of weeks.

Beyond engineering teams, Manulife is embedding AI across the organization, equipping employees with tools aimed at streamlining everyday work, unlocking productivity gains, and delivering greater value to customers. Manulife expects to generate more than $1 billion[i] of enterprise value by 2027, with $300 million achieved as of year-end 2025, improving productivity and efficiency and delivering real impact for customers, colleagues and shareholders.

“Our longstanding partnership with Manulife has always been grounded in trust, innovation and a shared commitment to responsible transformation,” said Matt Milton, President, Microsoft Canada. “We are proud to be Manulife’s trusted partner in the agentic era, helping empower employees with Microsoft 365 Copilot and scale AI responsibly with the governance and security of Microsoft Agent 365. We look forward to continuing our work together as Manulife turns AI into practical value and better outcomes for customers around the world.”

The partnership expansion reinforces Manulife’s position as an industry leader in AI innovation and underscores its commitment to becoming an AI‑driven organization. For two consecutive years, Manulife was recognized as the number one life insurance company in North America and Europe for AI maturity in the Evident AI Insurance Index. authors: Samantha Subin, www.facebook.com, MacKenzie Sigalos, Jonathan Vanian, Jordan Novet
description:
—Jordan Novet Google is trying to keep up with OpenAI and Anthropic with its cutting-edge Gemini AI models, while also offering models at prices that recognize a more frugal approach to AI spending.
On Tuesday, the company released three new Gemini models, including its clearest answer yet to Anthropic's lead in cybersecurity.
Second-quarter revenue in Alphabet's Google Cloud unit, which includes infrastructure and Google Workspace productivity subscriptions, is expected to show 64% growth from a year earlier to $22.24 billion, according to StreetAccount.
Large companies are running more apps on Google's cloud, incorporating the company's AI models, CEO Sundar Pichai said on the last earnings call in April.
In April, Google touted a cloud TPU for training AI models and one that handles inference jobs.
text:
Google's earnings come on the heels of some major high-profile departures, as the battle for top artificial intelligence talent heats up.

Gemini co-head Noam Shazeer announced in June that he was joining OpenAI, less than two years after returning through a partnership with his startup. Senior researcher scientist John Jumper left Google Deepmind for Anthropic last month.

Technology companies have spent billions in recent months to lure top talent and acquire AI capabilities. The frontier labs, however, are starting to face a new reality, as businesses begin reining in token costs and seek out cheaper alternatives.

Software companies have also fallen victim to the AI talent drain as frontier labs build out the enterprise layer.

—Samantha Subin

Investors will be paying attention to Alphabet's investment income after a recent Anthropic funding round pushed up the value of Google's holding in the model developer.

In 2023, Google first bought a 10% stake in Anthropic. The search company announced plans to invest up to $40 billion more in April, having invested more than $3 billion in the startup already. By May, with Anthropic's Claude Code gaining attention for its ability to quickly write application code, the company said investors had valued it at $965 billion. That was up from $380 billion as of February.

Alphabet is also sitting on a stake in SpaceX, which went public in June, after first investing $900 million in the rocket maker in 2015. SpaceX shares have drifted down about 8% since the record-setting initial public offering.

Three months ago, Google touted a $37 billion gain on equity securities.

—Jordan Novet

Google is trying to keep up with OpenAI and Anthropic with its cutting-edge Gemini AI models, while also offering models at prices that recognize a more frugal approach to AI spending.

On Tuesday, the company released three new Gemini models, including its clearest answer yet to Anthropic's lead in cybersecurity. Gemini 3.5 Flash Cyber is designed to detect and patch software vulnerabilities and will initially be available only to governments and trusted partners through a limited-access pilot. Google said the specialized model runs at a lower price per token than larger models.

With Gemini 3.6 Flash, Google aims to bolster its coding assistant technology while using up to 17% fewer tokens and offering a lower price per token than the previous model.

The pricing war in AI is heating up as demand soars for open-source models, largely out of China. The hottest recent example is Moonshot AI's Kimi K3.

— MacKenzie Sigalos

Google's stock is on pace for a third straight month as the company heads into the second-quarter print on mounting AI skepticism.

Shares are up 11% for the year but have dropped 1% in May, 6% in June and are pacing for a nearly 3% loss in July.

That puts the company behind Apple and Nvidia for the year.

Google's stock drop comes as skepticism swirls over skyrocketing artificial intelligence spending and businesses pour billions into the infrastructure buildout.

— Samantha Subin

Investors shouldn't expect Alphabet's epic spending spree to change course next year.

Finance chief Anat Ashkenazi said in April that 2027 capex is likely to "significantly increase" from the up to $190 billion planned for this year.

Evercore analysts wrote in a note over the weekend that "when the CFO warns about following year capex in the March Quarter, the plans are going to be aggressive." The Evercore analysts then — jokingly — asked if the number could hit "$300B? $350B?!"

Ultimately, they settled on an estimate of $262 billion, and noted that they're concerned "that capex spend could ramp higher than this." The consensus estimate for Alphabet's 2027 capex is about $257 billion, according to FactSet.

— Jonathan Vanian

Analysts expect YouTube's advertising revenue growth to ease up as the video engine reaches greater scale.

The unit should contribute $10.81 billion in revenue, which would imply roughly 10% growth from a year earlier, decelerating from 11% expansion in the first quarter.

In May, at the I/O developer conference, Google said YouTube had reached 3 billion users, alongside the company's search engine, Gmail, Chrome and Android. The milestone makes the site an increasingly compelling destination for advertisers.

Meta had 3.56 billion "daily active people" across its apps in the first quarter.

Evercore ISI analysts came away with a favorable assessment of YouTube's stature following a June survey. In a note to clients on Sunday, they pointed to relatively attractive advertising costs and "linear TV leakage."

—Jordan Novet

Google is trailing Amazon and Microsoft in cloud computing, but it's been growing faster.

Second-quarter revenue in Alphabet's Google Cloud unit, which includes infrastructure and Google Workspace productivity subscriptions, is expected to show 64% growth from a year earlier to $22.24 billion, according to StreetAccount.

That's an acceleration from 63% expansion in the first quarter, which topped market leader Amazon Web Services' 28% growth. At Microsoft, revenue from Azure and other cloud services increased 40%.

Large companies are running more apps on Google's cloud, incorporating the company's AI models, CEO Sundar Pichai said on the last earnings call in April. Additionally, the Gemini Enterprise assistant for corporate workers, which starts at $21 per person per month, is gaining traction, he said.

Demand for Google's tensor processing units, or TPUs, is also ramping at AI labs. In April, Google touted a cloud TPU for training AI models and one that handles inference jobs.

The $29.5 billion acquisition earlier this year of cloud security company Wiz is also boosting cloud growth. Google is seeing so much demand that it inked a deal in June with Elon Musk's SpaceX, agreeing to pay $920 million a month for AI compute capacity.

— Jordan Novet

Alphabet and its hyperscaler peers are spending boatloads of money on massive data center and related computing projects, and investors are paying close attention.

That puts a particular focus on Alphabet's capital expenditures, or capex, which has been skyrocketing in recent quarters. In April, the company raised its 2026 capex guidance to between $180 billion and $190 billion, up from $175 billion to $185 billion.

The consensus estimate for Alphabet's 2026 capex is $187.1 billion, according to FactSet. Among the web giants, Amazon is the only one expected to spend more, with analysts projecting capex of $200 billion, in line with the company's forecast.

— Jonathan Vanian

text:
Hertz, one of America's best-known car rental companies, is trying to position itself as the backbone of the robotaxi business.

Why it matters: As robotaxis scale, fleet operators — companies that can efficiently own, charge, clean and maintain self-driving vehicles — could become the industry's kingmakers.

Catch up quick: Hertz recently created a new business unit, Oro Mobility, to manage and service a range of fleets including ride-sharing and autonomous vehicles.

Its first big AV deal is to manage Uber's planned Lucid-Nuro robotaxi fleet launching later this year in San Francisco, with additional markets to follow.

Hertz, which has long rented cars to ride-share drivers, is also deploying 1,000 of its own employees to drive Hertz cars for Uber.

The big picture: It's all part of a strategy shift led by new CEO Gil West, who is pairing a back-to-basics turnaround of the car rental business with a long-term bet that Hertz's fleet-management expertise can power the next generation of mobility services.

"We're not a tech company, nor should we be, but we've got 100 years of experience owning and managing large fleets," West tells Axios.

State of play: Hertz is still trying to rebound from a disastrous bet on electric vehicles made just months after it emerged from bankruptcy in 2021.

The EV blunder cost Hertz close to $2 billion after poor customer experiences, surging repair costs and plunging resale values forced a massive sell-off of 30,000 EVs, most of them Teslas.

Yet the painful chapter also helped prepare Hertz for its next challenge — charging and maintaining electric robotaxis for AV partners.

Hertz's advantage is that it already owns much of the physical infrastructure robotaxi operators need.

It has more than 11,000 locations — including at 2,900 airports — in 160 countries, and already has 2,700 EV chargers installed.

Its rental fleet of more than half a million cars is worth over $12 billion.

"It would take somebody decades and billions of dollars to replicate what we have," West said.

The intrigue: West, who previously was chief operating officer at General Motors' Cruise robotaxi unit, acknowledges that managing a fleet of robotaxis is different from running a rental car business.

Having Hertz employees drive for Uber is an important stepping stone for developing the playbook, he said.

The program lets Hertz refine every aspect of fleet operations — dispatching, telematics, safety monitoring, cleaning cycles and charging schedules — before replacing drivers with software.

"We are really honing the muscle tone for autonomous ... it's an easy natural transition to go from this human-driven fleet to autonomous."

Yes, but: Hertz certainly isn't alone in recognizing the potential growth opportunity in robotaxi operations.

Lyft's Flexdrive fleet management unit is building an 80,000-square-foot Waymo hub in Nashville, while Avis Budget Group runs Waymo's Dallas depot.

Other key players include Avomo, which runs Waymo operations in Austin, Atlanta and Madrid, and Nigerian fintech Moove, which runs Phoenix and Miami for Waymo.

The bottom line: The robotaxi revolution's next layer isn't about technology; it's about scaling operations.
